events.description: Indians at Fort Peck were allotted approximately twelve years before the writing of this document
All Indians on the Coeur d'Alene reservation were allotted 160 acres of land each, including about 80 allotments to whites or near whites of French-Canadian extraction
First competency commission visited Snead's district; large number of applicants received orders for removal of restrictions
Act of Congress of May 27, 1908 removed restrictions of mixed blood Indians of the Five Civilized Tribes
Over four years, the superintendent allowed patents-in-fee to practically all young and middle aged people asking for it, recommending only a portion of their allotments in most cases
Over four years, approximately fifty homes were built for Indians who sold their land through the office
Edward P. Snead appeared before the Investigation Committee for the House Committee of Indian Affairs
Period of restriction for Choctaw Indians set to be terminated in 1931, causing great concern
During the last year, restrictions were placed on handling of Indian income, hoping to cause many to prefer farming their own land rather than renting it
Seventy-five percent of mixed-blood Indians of Hughes County were estimated to have been defrauded out of seventy percent of the value of their allotments

financial_transactions.description: In Hughes County, 1600 mixed blood allotments of 160 acres each were appraised at $1,040 each for allotment purposes; very small percent received fair consideration
Mollie Johnson, one-quarter blood Creek Roll No. 9130, executed deeds conveying her lands without receiving fair consideration; loss approximately $750
Daniel Johnson, one-quarter blood Creek Roll No. 9131, prevailed upon to deed away his land receiving practically nothing; loss $900
Adeline Grayson, one-half blood Creek, deluded into executing conveyances transferring her allotment without proper consideration
Henderson Arbor, one-quarter blood Creek Roll No. 9613, persuaded to sign conveyance on his allotment without adequate consideration; loss $850
Estimated total amount lost by 1600 mixed-blood Indians in Hughes County (eighty percent of 1600 times $1,040 times seventy percent)
Estimated total amount lost by 567 mixed-blood Indians in Seminole County (567 times $960)

correspondence.subject: Granting of patents-in-fee to Indian wards of the Government
correspondence.action_requested: Response to letter of the 31st ultimo regarding advisability of patents-in-fee
correspondence.outcome: Lawshe recommended against general issuance of patents-in-fee unless Indian has demonstrated self-supporting capacity through farming or gainful occupation

correspondence.subject: Advisability of releasing Indians from Government supervision
correspondence.action_requested: Response to April 2nd correspondence about releasing Indians from supervision
correspondence.outcome: Snead favored liberal policy of removal for competent Indians but adequate protection for those unable to handle own affairs; opposed blanket release

correspondence.subject: Releasing Indians from Government supervision - Creek and Seminole Indians
correspondence.action_requested: Views on releasing Indians from government supervision
correspondence.outcome: Youngblood favored holding restrictions on allotted land during lifetime of allottee; cited massive land fraud statistics

Investigation Committee examined extension of restriction period; indicated extension would be entertained only in case of absolute necessity

testimony.witness_title: Field Clerk, Idabel, Oklahoma; member of Choctaw tribe
testimony.hearing: Investigation Committee for the House Committee of Indian Affairs
testimony.subject: Extension of restriction period for Choctaw Indians and protection of Indian property
testimony.key_claims: Testified that extension of restriction period would be entertained only in case of absolute necessity; emphasized that failure to provide protection would further interests of those seeking to separate Indians from their property; expressed great concern about approaching 1931 termination of Choctaw restrictions

testimony.subject: Patent-in-fee policy and Indian competency
testimony.key_claims: Three-fourths of Nez Perce Indians are thrifty, sober and law abiding; Rocky Boy Indians demonstrate that 60 years of freedom without supervision led to degradation and poverty; opposed granting citizenship to Indians in bulk; recommended each case be considered on its own merit; in four years allowed patents-in-fee to practically all young and middle aged people asking but only recommended portions of allotments; in great majority of cases patentees did nothing; Indians have lived on children's moneys for four years and refuse to work; of 196 patents issued, 36 have nothing left, 13 built homes, 56 retained land

testimony.witness_title: Superintendent, Coeur d'Alene Indian Agency, Sorrento, Idaho
testimony.subject: Patents-in-fee policy and results at Coeur d'Alene Reservation
testimony.key_claims: Administration of Indian affairs is a trust or guardianship; government policy of rationing without requiring repayment pauperized American Indians; opposed patent-in-fee unless allottee has personally farmed and become self-supporting; of 139 patents-in-fee issued, 55 were to whites, 54 Indians sold or lost land through mortgages, 42 doing no good; one full-blood with little education purchased additional land and is farming successfully; usual practice when Indian receives patent is to mortgage the land; many Indians told him they wished they had never received their patent; automobile nearly as demoralizing to Indian as whiskey

testimony.subject: Results of releasing Creek and Seminole Indians from restrictions
testimony.key_claims: In Hughes County, 1600 mixed blood allotments valued at $1,040 each; very small percent received fair consideration; 75% of mixed-bloods defrauded of 70% of allotment value; total estimated loss $873,600 in Hughes County and $544,320 in Seminole County; described specific fraud cases including Mollie Johnson, Daniel Johnson, Adeline Grayson, and Henderson Arbor; land men commonly called grafters are demanding Indians be turned loose; honest hard-working farmers living among Indians do not want them turned loose; proper education is the only solution

mortgages.land_description: Original allotments on Coeur d'Alene Reservation
mortgages.context: 54 of 91 patents issued since 1916 were sold or lost through mortgages; many of the 56 who still have land have it badly mortgaged; ordinary method when patent is procured is to either sell the land, trade it for automobile, or mortgage it; mortgage proceeds would be more than the land's value, and foreclosure results
Many of the 56 Indians reported as still having their land have their land badly mortgaged

mortgages.land_description: Allotments in Hughes and Seminole Counties, Oklahoma
mortgages.context: Ninety percent of land is sold or encumbered for funds above the Indian's earning capacity who later are obliged to sell
